grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in present, change the dependent verb to imparfait.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb imparfait
usage: When reporting present tense statements with a past main clause
restrictions: Applies only when the main clause is in a past tense such as the passé composé
Requires the direct speech to be in the present tense
Not applied when the main clause is in the present, which keeps the present form
conditions: Direct speech is in present tense
Main clause is in passé composé
exceptions: When the main clause is in the present, the present is kept in the dependent clause
The imparfait marks the shift into indirect speech, not a habitual past meaning
agreement_rules: The tense shift from present to imparfait preserves subject-verb agreement in person and number.
Imparfait endings continue to mark person and number in the dependent clause.

sources.section_title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps
sources.source_text: la concordance des temps

In direct speech (le discours direct), one says something or asks a question directly. ... In indirect speech (le discours indirect), the words of one or more people are reported or a question is asked indirectly.

sections.title: Main clause verbs in indirect speech

sources.section_title: Main clause verbs in indirect speech
sources.source_text: Verbs in the main clause of indirect speech are followed by que (où, si, etc.); the verb in the dependent clause is usually in the indicative. Here are some typical main clause verbs: affirmer, annoncer, assurer, avouer, confier, constater, crier, déclarer, dire, expliquer, observer, prétendre, promettre, remarquer, répondre, révéler, s'apercevoir, savoir, se rendre compte.

sections.title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps

sources.section_title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps
sources.source_text: Learning la concordance des temps, that is, balancing tenses, is one of the most difficult tasks of a French learner. When switching from direct to indirect speech, some changes of tense occur when the main clause verb is in the passé composé.
